3) If there’s no leak (pipe just frozen), the usual safe approach is:
- Turn the faucet on slightly (the one the frozen pipe feeds) so it’s open and ready to drip.
- Use gentle heat at the frozen section only:
  - A hair dryer on low/medium, moving it back and forth along the pipe.
  - Or a heating pad wrapped around the pipe.
  - Or towels soaked in warm (not boiling) water, wrapped around and refreshed as they cool.
- Do NOT use: open flame, propane torch, or boiling water on the pipe.

Reply with:
1) Leak or no leak?
2) House/apartment ZIP or city (so I know how severe the cold is, and we can get a plumber if needed)?
3) What you have available (hair dryer, space heater, heating pad, etc.)?

I’ll then give you precise next steps tailored to your situation, and if you want, I can help you line up a plumber in case the pipe is cracked or won’t thaw.</action>

<action type="say">
Got it—no leak yet is good news. Let’s try to thaw this carefully.

1) Prep and safety
- Open the cabinet doors fully under the sink.
- Clear out anything flammable (paper, cleaners, plastic bags) so the space heater and hair dryer aren’t near them.
- Turn the affected faucet ON slightly (just a small open stream position, even if nothing comes out). This gives melting ice somewhere to go.

2) Use the space heater
- Place the space heater several feet away from the cabinet, pointed into the open cabinet doors.
- Use a low/medium setting so you gently warm the area; don’t blast high heat right up against the pipes or cabinet.
- Make sure the heater is on a stable surface with nothing blocking it, and that you can keep an eye on it (don’t leave the apartment or fall asleep with it running).

3) Targeted heat with the hair dryer
- Look for the section of pipe most likely against or near the exterior wall—often that’s where it’s frozen.
- Start with the hair dryer on low/medium, about 6–8 inches away from the pipe.
- Move the dryer slowly back and forth along the pipe—don’t just park it in one spot.
- If you see any shutoff valves or bends/elbows near the cold wall, focus more time there; those are common freeze points.
- Continue this for 15–20 minutes at a time, then check the faucet.

4) What you should see
- As the ice starts to melt, the faucet may begin to drip or sputter air/water. That’s a good sign; keep the water running slowly as it improves.
- Watch under the sink for any beads of water forming on the pipe, joints, or valves. If you see a steady drip or spray that wasn’t there before, turn off the main water right away if you can, and close that faucet.

5) If it won’t thaw
- Sometimes it can take 30–60 minutes of on-and-off heating in very cold conditions.
- If after that you still have no flow, or a section of pipe is completely inaccessible (e.g., inside the wall) it’s wise to bring in a plumber before the line splits as temps fluctuate.

If you want, I can:
- Help you keep pipes from refreezing after it thaws (important in Minneapolis), and/or
- Look up available plumbers near downtown Minneapolis and line up someone on routine or same-day basis.

For now, start the heater + hair dryer steps and tell me:
- After 15–20 minutes, do you get any dripping or sputtering at the faucet?
- Do you see any moisture forming on the pipe or around joints under the sink?</action>

<action type="say">
A bulged section is a strong sign the pipe wall is damaged or very close to it. When it finally thaws and pressure returns, that’s the most likely place for it to burst.

Do this now:

1) Get ready to shut off the water
- Find your main shutoff and make sure you can reach it quickly.
  - House/condo: often in the basement, utility room, or near where the main water line comes in / water meter.
  - Apartment: sometimes in a closet, behind an access panel near the kitchen/bath, or there may only be a building/main valve.
- If you’re in an apartment/condo and don’t know where it is, call building maintenance and tell them:
  “I have a frozen pipe under my kitchen sink with a visible bulge. It may burst when it thaws. I need to know where the shutoff is or have someone check it.”

2) Change how you’re heating (or pause)
Because of the bulge:
- Do NOT blast high heat directly on that swollen spot.
- If you continue at all:
  - Keep the space heater at a safe distance, just gently warming the cabinet area.
  - Use the hair dryer only on low/medium, moving it along the pipe and not parked on the bulge.
  - Stay there watching the pipe the whole time, ready to shut off the main immediately.

If you feel unsure or can’t easily get to the shutoff, it’s safer to stop trying to thaw it yourself and get a plumber so they can open the wall/pipe and control the thaw and repair.

3) If water starts
- If you see a spray, stream, or fast drip from that bulged area or a nearby joint:
  - Immediately shut off the main water.
  - Put a bucket/towels under the area if you can safely.
  - Don’t turn the water back on until the damaged section is repaired.

If you’d like, I can help you line up a plumber in downtown Minneapolis next:
- Are you in a rented apartment/condo or a place you own?
- Do you want emergency/as-soon-as-possible service, or can this be handled later today/next available?

Once you answer those, I can look up options and help you get someone scheduled.</action>
